title: Three Changes: A Simple Reflection Practice
markdown:
# Three Changes: A Simple Reflection Practice

## Why Small Changes Matter

Much of daily life moves in small shifts rather than large events. A room changes temperature. A conversation changes tone. A thought arrives and then leaves. Noticing these shifts is a form of everyday self-reflection that does not require a special setting or a long block of time. It asks only that you pause and name what is different from a moment before.

This exercise is adapted from an English-language guided reflection ebook. Digital access is sold through the owned checkout page. The practice below is presented here so you can try it today without needing anything else.

## The Practice: Three Changes

You need paper or a notes app, a pen, and about six minutes.

Step 1: Pick a transition point
Choose a regular moment in your day, such as midday, after work, or before bed. A consistent time makes the habit easier to remember, but a single try is enough to see how it works.

Step 2: Set a short timer
Six minutes is enough. A timer keeps the writing from turning into a long journal entry. When the time ends, stop even if you feel you have more to say.

Step 3: Name three changes
Write down three small changes you observed today. They can be external or internal. Examples include:
- The light in the kitchen was bright at breakfast and dim by dinner.
- Your email inbox had twenty messages in the morning and five in the afternoon.
- Your shoulders felt tight after a meeting and looser after a walk.

Write each change as a short phrase. Do not judge whether the change was good or bad.

Step 4: Add a before and after
For each of the three changes, write one sentence about what was there before and one sentence about what is there now. Keep the sentences factual.
Example:
Before: The coffee cup was full and steaming.
After: The cup is empty and cool.

This before-and-after structure anchors the abstract idea of impermanence in something you can see or feel.

Step 5: Read the list once and close it
Read what you wrote without adding commentary. Then close the notebook or app. You do not need to act on the list. You do not need to solve anything. The practice ends when you close the page.

## An Example

Here is what a completed entry might look like.

Change 1: The sky outside my window.
Before: Gray clouds covered the sky at lunchtime.
After: The clouds had broken and a strip of blue appeared by late afternoon.

Change 2: The stack of mail on the hall table.
Before: Five envelopes sat in a pile when I left the house.
After: Three envelopes remain; two were opened and recycled.

Change 3: My breathing while sitting at the desk.
Before: My breath was shallow and fast after a phone call.
After: My breath is slower and deeper now.

The writer did not explain why the clouds moved or why the mail was opened. They only recorded what changed.

## Keeping It Simple

If six minutes feels like too much, start with three minutes and one change. If paper is not handy, use a notes app. The goal is not to produce a perfect record but to practice noticing that things are different from one moment to the next.

You can repeat this at any transition, or only when you remember. There is no required streak and no score. The reflection is complete when you have named three changes and closed the page.
